title: A hymn in Gauri
hook: Gauri holds Sukhmani and the Bavan Akhri

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Gauri, the earnest raga that runs page after page, and your line was earnest and deep. Today, two long compositions that live inside it.

Peace of mind has a name in the Guru Granth Sahib, and an address. The name is Sukhmani. The address is a heading on ang two hundred sixty-two: Gauri Sukhmani, Mahala five. A whole block of year two walked through it. But it's easy to forget the first word of that heading, the one a singer reads before anything else. Before it's Sukhmani, it's Gauri.
screen: `PEACE OF MIND HAS A NAME.` → `GAURI SUKHMANI, MAHALA FIVE.` → `BEFORE SUKHMANI, GAURI.`

segments.voice: Sukhmani is Guru Arjan's, and it's long: section after section, each opened by a salok. Its first ashtapadi begins with remembering. In paraphrase: remembering, remembering, I find peace. And its rahao says what the name means: Sukhmani, peace, the nectar of the Lord's Name, which comes to rest in the minds of devotees. The composition defines itself. Now hear it as a Gauri hymn. A composition that wants to settle a restless mind, slowly, over a long stretch, is at home in that earnest, unhurried sound. The raga gives Sukhmani its pace before the words give it its meaning. A few pages earlier in Gauri sits a different kind of long hymn, also Guru Arjan's: the Bavan Akhri. It walks through the alphabet one letter at a time, giving a teaching for each, the way a child learns letters, a word for every sound. Kabir has a Bavan Akhri in Gauri too, further on in the section. So Gauri holds two of the Granth's patient shapes: peace, built section by section, and wisdom, built letter by letter. Both take time, and Gauri gives them time. Look back at the week: the order of the ragas, thirty-one moods; Sri Rag and its hymn, which watch now; Majh and its letters of longing; Gauri, earnest and deep, and today, peace in gauri. Tomorrow the list moves on to Asa.
screen: `SUKHMANI DEFINES ITSELF: PEACE, THE NAME.` · `GAURI GIVES IT ITS PACE.` · `THE BAVAN AKHRI: LETTER BY LETTER.` · then, large: `PEACE IN GAURI.`

segments.voice: If you can, let the opening of Sukhmani, sung in Gauri, play through the sit without chasing the meaning. Otherwise make its first idea a breath, remembering on the way in, peace on the way out, slower than feels natural, and when a thought pulls you away, come back as if starting the next section. If you pray, let the breath carry Waheguru instead.
A hymn in Gauri. Sukhmani, Guru Arjan's long hymn of peace, and the Bavan Akhri, teaching letter by letter, both set in Gauri's earnest pace. Today's word.
Your line: peace in gauri. Peace built section by section, wisdom built letter by letter. That's the week.

howItsDone: Sukhmani Sahib is recited in Sikh homes and gurdwaras, by individuals or by groups, and is also sung in kirtan in Raag Gauri; the Bavan Akhri is read as part of the Gauri section of the Guru Granth Sahib.

what a scholar hears: Sukhmani (Gauri Sukhmani M5, from Ang 262) is built of ashtapadis each opened by a salok, and its rahao glosses the title; nearby Guru Arjan's Bavan Akhri (Ang 250) and, later, Kabir's (Ang 340) are acrostics on the letters of the alphabet, all within the Gauri section.

chat.says: Sukhmani is a prayer for peace, right? So why does its heading start with 'Gauri'?
options: It's the raga: Gauri's earnest, unhurried pace suits a hymn that slowly settles the mind.
Gauri was the name of the person Guru Arjan first wrote Sukhmani for, long ago.
Gauri is a place, the town where Sukhmani was first sung aloud in public.

rahao.meaning: pause, stay: the mark after a hymn's refrain
